footer: All data come from free public APIs (wheretheiss / Celestrak / NOAA SWPC / NASA NEO / NASA Exoplanet Archive / Launch Library 2) for popular-science and visualization only, not for navigation or engineering. Station and satellite pass positions are TLE + SGP4 estimates and differ from measurements; moon phase is computed by a local astronomical algorithm.
adviceExcellent: Excellent conditions tonight—observe or photograph now
adviceGood: Good conditions, ideal for visual observing
adviceFair: Moonlight or disturbance is strong; pick faint targets
earthMoonNote: Moon phase follows from Earth–Moon–Sun geometry and needs no network—correct time is enough. At perigee the Moon looks ~14% larger than at apogee and tides are stronger.
earthStationSource: wheretheiss.at (live ISS) + Celestrak (TLE), local SGP4 propagation
earthNoVisible: All stations are on the far side now
earthPassSource: TLE + SGP4 local propagation (same elements as the station panel)
earthPassLoading: Computing visible passes over {city} in the next 6 hours… (no result means targets are on the far side or below the horizon)
sunSwNote: When Bz is negative the solar wind more easily triggers geomagnetic storms, raising GPS and grid risks. The chain is: Bz turns negative + solar wind speeds up → magnetosphere compresses → energy pours in → Kp rises → G-scale alert.
sunFlareSource: NOAA SWPC GOES 1-min long band (0.05–0.4nm) X-ray flux; flares identified locally
sunFlareEmpty: No B-class+ flares in the last 24h (quiet Sun)
sunProtonSource: NOAA SWPC GOES integrated proton flux, multi-satellite merged by max timestamp
sunAuroraSource: NOAA SWPC OVATION aurora model inversion (multi-satellite fusion)
sunAuroraNote: The criterion compares geographic latitude with the aurora oval's southern edge ({edge}°). Mohe lies north of {edge}° and may see it during active periods; Beijing (40°N) is below that latitude and needs a G4+ storm to push the oval south.
sunCycleSource: NOAA SWPC observations + official prediction range (25%/75% confidence)
sunCycleNote: Solar activity follows an ~11-year cycle. The current Cycle 25 began in late 2019; the observed smoothed peak is {smoothed} ({month}). The band on the curve is NOAA's official prediction interval—narrower means more confidence.
sunAlertSource: NOAA SWPC alerts product, parsed into level/intensity/impact
sunAlertEmpty: No space-weather alerts in the last 72h (quiet)
skyCondSource: Sun altitude sampled locally from subsolar geometry (−18° = astronomical night boundary, IAU); observing index = moonlight 40% + darkness 35% + geomagnetic 25%
skyChartSource: Catalog d3-celestial (HYG/Hipparcos, 5044 stars brighter than mag 6 + 89 constellation lines + 110 Messier objects); positions computed locally
skyMeteorSource: IMO generic shower parameters (local data); moonlight interference computed from peak-night moon phase locally
messierEmpty: No Messier objects above the horizon now (try another city or wait for dark)
galaxyNote: Schematic, not to scale · Sun orbits the center in ≈ {n} yr
apodTitle: NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD)
apodSource: NASA APOD (apod.nasa.gov), one per day, curated by NASA; server-cached and forwarded for 3h
apodEmpty: APOD temporarily unavailable (NASA DEMO_KEY rate limit or network error)
deepGalaxyTitle: Milky Way Structure & the Sun's Position
deepGalaxySource: ESA Gaia DR3 public data / NASA Milky Way parameters
cometCometSource: NASA JPL Small-Body Database (curated list, elements refreshed every 24h)
cometCometLead: Comets have eccentricity near 1 (very flat orbits) with tiny perihelion and huge aphelion—that is why they only grow tails during the few months near the Sun, and are dim dirty snowballs the rest of the time.
cometAsteroidLead: Unlike comets, asteroids have small eccentricity and near-circular orbits. These are the few visited up close or even sampled by probes—their diameters and albedos are measured, not estimated.
cometFailed: {n} bodies failed to load (upstream unavailable; auto-retried on refresh):
cometPerTip: Time to orbit the Sun. Comets: decades to millennia; asteroids: mostly 3–6 yr
apprDiamTip: Order-of-magnitude estimate from H at albedo 0.14, not a measured diameter
apprSource: NASA JPL Close Approach Data (within 0.05 AU, sorted by distance)
apprLead1: Bodies in this table all pass
apprLeadBold1: inside or near the Moon's orbit
apprLead2: by Earth. Most are only ~10s of meters—they burn up high if they enter; the real concern is
obsSource: Open-Meteo live (cloud / visibility / precipitation), refresh every 10 min
obsLead2: , not moon phase or light pollution: a full moon raises the sky background so even a score of 100 hides faint nebulae. Compare with the moon/planet data in "Tonight's Sky".
obsAdviceExcellent: Clear and transparent—Milky Way and deep-sky objects visible to the naked eye
obsAdviceGood: Observable; planets and bright stars are fine
obsAdviceFair: Cloudy; only the Moon and bright stars
obsAdvicePoor: Mostly clouded over; try another night
obsAdviceBad: Rain or fog; not suitable for observing
obsAdviceNodata: No live data for this city
caseArtemisDesc: Artemis I is the first step of the return-to-Moon program: the SLS rocket sent the Orion spacecraft into a lunar orbit to verify life support and deep-space communications. It maps to the launch tracking in the "Launches" tab—every launch is a replayable orbit curve.
caseChange6Desc: Chang'e 6 landed and sampled in the lunar far-side South Pole–Aitken basin, returning to Earth via the Queqiao-2 relay—the first sample ever retrieved from the far side. It echoes the moon-phase/lunar data in "Tonight's Sky": the satellite we watch is being unveiled bit by bit.
caseSolarMaxDesc: Solar activity follows an ~11-year cycle; at maximum, spots, flares and CMEs erupt frequently. The "Solar Activity" tab plots sunspot number and flare level in real time, where you can see the rise and fall with the solar cycle—the root cause of recent frequent auroras at high latitudes.

solarSource: JPL Standish approximate orbital elements (computed locally), epoch J2000, valid 1800–2050
solarFoot: Sunlight takes {min} minutes to cross 1 AU (8 min 20 s) · the geocentric distance of inner planets varies with phase: perihelion ≈0.983 AU, aphelion ≈1.017 AU
neoSource: NASA NeoWs (Near Earth Object Web Service, DEMO_KEY)
